utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Alex Demirdjian on behalf of the Prosecutor, with Senior Trial Attorney Tom Hannis and our Case Manager Mr. Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Before Mr. Demirdjian resumes his examination-in-chief, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just before I resume with my questions, a little correction for the transcript: Yesterday at page 12394, line 8, we were talking about uniforms, and it was registered as "SNB uniforms." That's wrong. It's "SMB," M as in Mary. That's how it should be recorded, and that's the camouflage -- the olive-grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Raljic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to talk about the communication devices available to the various units present in Kotor Varos. And yesterday you mentioned to us one group which was Ljuban Ecim's special police that was present in Kotor Varos. To your knowledge, how would they communicate with their superiors?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they only had hand-held radio stations. Which model, I cannot say. Whether it was Motorola or something else, I really wouldn't know. But they were hand-held radio stations for VHF communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know if they ever used the communications system at the SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, they would use the phone line when it was functional, but that unit was not in a position to use that communication system. If they worked on simplex communications, they would use their hand-held radio stations. And as far as I know, that was their basic means of communication, or their main means of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were you present -- were you ever present when they made a call from the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that they would use the phone lines when it was functional. Which phone line would they use, and which part of the SJB building would they go to use the phone line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was mostly at the duty officer's office. They had their phone lines. And that room was in the -- on the ground floor, very close to the entrance into the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to the subordinated units of the SJB. I believe there were smaller police stations in the municipality. Could you tell us how they communicated with the SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they weren't police stations, really; they were station departments. We had one at Siprage, but that was closed down. And there was a smaller department at Maslovare and another at Vrbanjci. As for communicating with them, if the repeater was functional, or, in other words when there was electrical power, we could use semi-duplex through the repeater and we could establish communications with Vrbanjci and Maslovare, but it was a problem to establish communications with Siprage because that place was some 30 kilometres away from Kotor Varos and the -- the terrain didn't allow for establishment of VHF communication with them. So we couldn't communicate with the station department of the police at Siprage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, would these smaller stations send reports to the police -- to the SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oral reports were not sent by radio communication. They also couldn't send dispatches. Whether or not written reports, that is, typewritten reports were made and subsequently transmitted, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, ultimately, how did you communicate with substations such as Siprage, where you told us that for a period of time you couldn't communicate with them? What would be the best way to communicate with them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the only way was going there in person. That is, sit in a car and driving there. That was the only way. Occasionally maybe, with the weather conditions permitting, we were sometimes able to establish communication with Siprage, but the quality of the communication was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the repeater. Where was the repeater located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on Mount Obodnik. That's some 12 or 13 kilometres from Kotor Varos, in the direction of Maslovare.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who controlled the area around Mount Obodnik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which area you mean. You mean the immediate vicinity around the repeater or the wider area?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The immediate vicinity around the repeater.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody actually secured that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And that area was -- around Mount Obodnik, who would main -- who was responsible for the maintenance of the repeater?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was something that must be repaired, there were the guys from the encryption department, encryption and maintenance department, from Banja Luka. They had an organisational unit in charge of system maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, in 1992, was that repeater ever damaged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The repeater often didn't work. It had -- it needed 220 volts to function, but I don't remember anyone going there for repairing anything in 1992. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just so we're clear on this, the repeater was used for what type of communications exactly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used for the same kind of communication as the hand-held radio stations when you work on simplex. When you work in simplex, there is a direct communication between two parties. Whereas, the repeater is actually an intermediary means of communication between the two parties, so we used the repeater when we wanted to establish communication between two points that were further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that under normal conditions you would use the repeater to communicate with Siprage, which was about 30 kilometres away. And you told us that Banja Luka was also 30 kilometres away. So under normal conditions, would you be able to establish communications between Banja Luka and Kotor Varos with this mean of communication?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that under normal conditions we were able to communicate with Siprage because we couldn't, by means of that repeater. But under specific conditions, because radio waves are very particular, depending on ionisation and the ionosphere and so on, so when the conditions were favourable, we, on rare occasions, were able to communicate with Siprage; that's what I said. But we couldn't connect with Banja Luka through that repeater because it's also some 30 kilometres away from Kotor Varos. But the Obodnik repeater is in the opposite direction, which means some 43 or 44 kilometres from Banja Luka. That was not a network through which we would communicate with Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Within the municipality of Kotor Varos itself, we have come to learn that there were various detention centres after the 11th of June. I'd like to ask you, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, before we change the subject, could we just explore with the witness what the situation was when there was a power cut. I think you touched on it yesterday, but since we are now speaking about the repeaters --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- and I think that Mr. Raljic already mentioned that sometimes the repeater didn't work, because they were out of power. How often did that happen, and what did they do when the power failed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, you heard Judge Harhoff's question. What would happen when the repeater was off? What would you do? First of all, maybe a first question: Would there be an attempt to fix the repeater?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wouldn't be considered a failure of the repeater. There is no need to go out there and repair anything because there isn't anything to repair. As I said, the repeater needed 220 volts AC to function. When there was a power failure, the repeater would switch off and we couldn't establish communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was the alternative to using the repeater? If you wanted to communicate, let's say, with Banja Luka, what was left for you in the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we didn't communicate with Banja Luka through that repeater. We were able to communicate with Vrbanjci and Maslovare because these places are some 10 to 20 kilometres from Kotor Varos and the repeater is between Vrbanjci and Maslovare. So it was used mostly for communicating with these two branch police stations. The alternative was to sit in a car and drive to Maslovare or Vrbanjci if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify something in relation to the communications with Siprage. You remember, when you arrived on Sunday, we gave you the opportunity to listen to the audio tapes of your interview in, in 2007. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the following day you had some corrections to make to that interview, or some clarifications; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that the rest of the interview was quite accurate.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I listened to about 80 per cent of the recording, which means I didn't listen to all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the part of the interview where communications with Siprage was discussed, and this was towards the end of the interview, and you were discussing a macro network?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And during the interview, do you remember telling us that you used this network mainly to communicate with Siprage which was 30 kilometres away from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what I said, but I didn't say that we were constantly able to communicate that way. Only with weather permitting, as I have just explained. Then we would be able to communicate with Siprage. But not otherwise. That's why I said that we communicated with Siprage that way because there was no other alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at the end of your answer you also said that you could establish communication through CSB Banja Luka. Maybe there is a misunderstanding here of what network you used, because you were talking about a macro network to communicate with Siprage. And then you said, We could also establish communication with CSB Banja Luka. Could you clarify that for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, sir. There was another frequency that could be used for communicating with the CSB and that was the macro network, the largest network that we could use. But the repeater was not on Obodnik, it was on Mount Kozara; we didn't speak about that. And that repeater either worked on channel 44 or channel 60. I'm not sure. And that's how we could communicate with Banja Luka, but not through the Obodnik repeater. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, does that clarify or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Except one little thing; namely, in the months between April and September 1992, roughly speaking, how often did you experience power cuts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On average, daily. Sometimes we would have electricity for five or ten days, but on other occasions there would be failures five to ten times a day. There were power failures all the time. I don't really remember a period of ten to 15 days with electricity. And speaking about the period from the 11th of June on. And in April and May, there were also power failures but not as often as later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you recall by any chance the longest period that you experienced without any power at all? In other words, how long would the power cuts normally last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think up to ten days. Because even the batteries would die that were used for feeding the VHF radio stations in the duty officer's room, and those batteries were strong enough for four to five days. Then we would take the battery to the adjacent where building where the military was and we would charge the battery using their generator so that we could use the battery again for -- to feed the radio stations. So the longest period was up to ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, I would like to turn to the topic of the communications that were available at the various detention centres in the municipality of Kotor Varos. And it is an established fact in this case that there were detention centres. Can you tell us what communication means were available there? And perhaps, when discussing it, if you can specify which detention centres you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I believe my learned friend should establish first the knowledge of this witness concerning the detention centres and only then ask the -- the question along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because it was my understanding that you wanted to establish that at the very beginning and then His Honour Judge Harhoff posed a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, you heard the question. Were you aware of the existence of detention centres in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not really familiar with the terminology. I cannot really tell whether it -- what there was -- can be called a detention centre or something else. But passing by the primary school or, rather, the gymnasium of the primary school, I saw a group of civilians, up to 100 persons, who were standing there. I don't know what they were doing or who had brought them there. We spoke about the building behind the pharmacy and some people were detained there. But I never saw them; they were behind closed doors. And that's what I know about that. I mean, first hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, who was guarding these various locations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the guards were. Around the primary school, there were many people wearing different uniforms because the triangle that -- that's made up of the prime school the police station and the university building as it was called, held by the military, are in a circle of 50 metres [Realtime transcript read in error "kilometres"] in diameter. There were many soldiers there those days in olive-drab uniforms and camouflage uniforms. There was police, special police. Many people. And by the entrance, and there's a hallway between the primary school building and the gymnasium the one through which I went, I think that there was a young man wearing an olive-drab uniform standing by the entrance. But whether or not he was a guard, I cannot say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At page 10, line 17, the witness said "50 metres," and it is recorded as "50 kilometres" in diameter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge -- now, you said there was all these various people guarding these locations, now, to your knowledge, was anyone using any device from the SJB at these locations to communicate with the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that various people moved about in the triangle between these buildings. But I don't know that anybody used means of communication from our station there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were there -- well, let me raise it this way. If have you -- if you have a patrol on the ground, what kind of communications means do they have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police patrols, if they went out on the beat, they would merely have hand-held radio stations, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that in the police chief's office he had a fax machine, a telephone line, and a hand-held radio. Would he be able to communicate with his hand-held radio to the police patrol on the ground who had a hand-held radio?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As long as we're talking about the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in the town itself, were you aware whether any member of the state security was present in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I would sometimes meet Zdravko Peic, and I think that he was a state security man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was he stationed in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He travelled from Banja Luka to Kotor Varos by car, as far as I know. Because, at the time, Zdravko lived in Banja Luka. I believe that he had an apartment there. But he hails from Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, how often would he come to Kotor Varos from Banja Luka by car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with any degree of certainty, but I would see him maybe once a week or twice a week, depending on which period we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Referring to a period after the takeover, the 11th of June, 1992, until the end of the year. How often would you see him in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant that period, but what I -- what I had in mind was whether we're talking about July or August or September or -- or any other time, until the end of the year. I -- sometimes I would meet him more often, sometimes less often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, how would he communicate -- or was there ever a need to communicate with Banja Luka; and, if so, how would he communicate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he wanted to communicate in that way, he would call us on the phone, if the phone lines were functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. 12, line 13, I don't think it was recorded as witness said. I believe the witness said that he would come to them and use the telephone if the telephone line was -- I don't know if it's important for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, if you would like to repeat your answer, how would Mr. Peic communicate with Banja Luka, if he needed to? Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if he needed to, he would drop by and use the phone, if the phone was functional, because of the frequent power failures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Next topic. Your chief, Mr. Savo Tepic, was responsible to the CSB Banja Luka chief, Mr. Zupljanin. To your knowledge, did Mr. Zupljanin visit or inspect the SJB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. Zupljanin, at sometime in the spring of 1992, did come. I think I saw him once in front of the SJB. And after the 11th of June, he may have been there, but I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, if he came to the SJB, would he have meetings in the SJB with the police chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he came to the SJB, it was logical for him to meet with the chief of the SJB. But if they really met at the SJB, I don't know. As I said, I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what was the relationship between Mr. Tepic and his superior, Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, because I drove the chief to Banja Luka to meetings in the previous period rather often, I know that they had good relations as professionals, but I believe that also they were in good relations personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did Mr. Tepic follow his boss's orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness said it -- well, first of all, which period of time is covered by. And I think it's calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The question is to his knowledge, from what he observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see Mr. Krgovic's -- the reason for his objection. But I suppose the witness could attempt to answer the question, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Maybe if I can rephrase it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, being in the communications department yourself, during the year 1992, you were receiving dispatches from CSB Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us you forwarded those dispatches to Mr. Tepic, your chief.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: From what you observed, did Mr. Tepic implement those orders or those dispatches that were coming in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that Chief Tepic was a professional and that he acted in coordination with subordination in the Ministry of the Interior. Now whether he specifically carried out certain orders or not, it was not my task to know that. But I was never issued an order by Chief Tepic which had to do with any specific dispatch, so I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was there ever a situation, to your knowledge, where Mr. Tepic did not follow orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, isn't this -- it's -- I think you've gone as far as you can with that with the witness's previous answer, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'll move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, we know that in 1992 there was in existence a Crisis Staff in Kotor Varos. You were aware of their existence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would anyone from the police station attend meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief Tepic would sometimes go to the meetings of the Crisis Staff. Whether he went there regularly or just occasionally, and under what circumstances, is something that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what was the relationship between the police and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean relations between Chief Tepic or police in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The police in general.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question because I cannot say what was the relation of the entire police force with the Crisis Staff. The question is somewhat abstract.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand. To your knowledge, did the police have to submit any reports to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not. There was not a single report sent out to the Crisis Staff through the communications centre. Now, whether Chief Tepic would tell them anything orally is something that I do not know because I did not attend any of the Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know of any situation where Chief Tepic would receive orders from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us earlier about a few detention centres that you were able to observe. Do you know what was the ethnicity of the people detained there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only suppose that these were people of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity. But that is just something I'm supposing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the police station itself, did it have any cells?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station did not have cells. It did not have a prison department, but it had a detention unit which is close to the entrance of the building, and it is a detention unit that exists to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And after the 11th of June, did you know whether anyone was detained there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some people who were held in this room. Now whether they were imprisoned or detained, that's questionable. But I did see some people there when I was entering the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did you ever hear anything about the conditions of the detention in the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I cannot say anything about the conditions of detention except for the fact that it was a small room, not more than 10 square metres. So you can judge by yourself how many people could be placed there, maybe five or six or seven. Five or six metres from this room is a toilet. And I cannot say with any certainty how long these people spent there and what the sanitary and other conditions of their stay were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Being yourself in the police station, did you hear anything about the way they were treated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were rumours going around that some of the specials were a bit more brutal with these peoples. But this was just the talk going around, as it is a small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were there any notorious cases in these occurrences of being brutal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot mention any specific example from the police station where some of the people were detained. I cannot mention any such example.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of an event that happened on the 25th of June in front of the hospital in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, before you go on to another incident, could the witness explain what he means with "the specials."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, could you clarify once again for us what you meant by "the specials."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this period, we called the men who wore camouflage uniforms and had hats on their heads, we used to call them "specials."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is this the unit that you described to us yesterday as wearing light camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the light camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is this the group that you told us yesterday that was led by Mr. Dubocanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Does that clarify the matter, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And just one other detail. The witness says that in that room there could be normally five, six, to seven people. Would it be possible to accommodate more -- more or less normally 12 people in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the detention unit is meant to hold two to three people under normal circumstances. Now, whether you could put as many people in there, yes, if they were all standing, there could be a dozen of people in there. Ten people could be there. They couldn't sit down and they couldn't lie down, but if they were all standing there could be ten of them. I never counted them though, so I cannot be specific about the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, I alert you that you have 15 minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I plan on finishing within those 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: MR. Raljic, were you aware of an event that occurred in front of the hospital in Kotor Varos on the 25th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk going around the town on the following days about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what occurred exactly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what exactly happened. I heard that some people lost their lives, that they were killed; but what the number was, I wouldn't know, and I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that the following days there was talk in the town. Was there any talk about who committed the crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Some specials were mentioned, once again, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: With regard to these events - not only the hospital but also the detention - to your knowledge, was this ever reported by your chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the specific incidents that we mentioned; or, generally speaking, did he report anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, did he report any of the behaviour you've been describing to us so far, by the specials?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, I cannot say with certainty when that was, whether it was in the second half of June or so, as far as I remember, the chief sent a dispatch in which he noted that the specials had resorted to violence against some people and against himself personally. He said that he had some problems with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, where was this sent to, this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that dispatch was sent to the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that "the specials had resorted to violence against himself." Did that occur before the dispatch was sent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he said that they behaved in a nasty manner towards him, even before the dispatch was sent, and there were problems with the specials. On one occasion, one of them kicked him in the belly in -- on the premises of the police station and seized his official pistol and so on, and all of this was done in front of other employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was there any consequence after he sent this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Consequence for whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were, first of all, any measures taken, to your knowledge, against these specials?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if any specific measures were taken, because these were armed men who were ready to do anything, and I'm not sure who would have been able to take any measures about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, until when did the specials remain in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was until around the month of September or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you sent that dispatch, you said maybe towards the second half of June; to your knowledge, was that dispatch received in Banja Luka? Was it a successful dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch was received by the communications centre in Banja Luka. Now where it was then sent further on from the communications centre is something that I couldn't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You remember yesterday you were talking about the ethnic makeup in the police station. I want to ask you what was the situation after the 11th of June. You told us that it was mixed. What was it after the 11th of June?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 11th of June, there were fewer people of other ethnicities who remained employed. As far as I remember, everything was blocked, and everything stopped for a couple of days. I cannot remember whether some people started working immediately or later, but I can remember that Sejdo Tatar and Jasmin Bajic continued working. I cannot remember when others began coming to work once again after the 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall a man by the name of Ilija Dragulic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What was his role? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Dragulic was a policeman who most frequently worked in -- was in charge of the traffic, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if anything happened to him after the 11th of June?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that Ilija was killed. I'm not sure how long after the 11th of June that was, whether it was 20 days or a month later, but I heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that Kotor Varos was a small town. Was there any word as to who perpetrated the crime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some rumours about that. But I can connect that with an incident which took place in the Kotor settlement. It was still peaceful at the time in this settlement, as far as I remember. Some people were handing over weapons their weapons, and there was a group of young men from some surrounding villages from the area around Kotor Varos who were standing guard there. One night someone through a hand-grenade in the room where they were. Some of these young men were killed on that occasion. And I think that the incident can be connected with Ilija Dragulic's death because on the following day, or soon thereafter, he lost his life and there were rumours going around that that group was involved in the incident of his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us about the actions of the specials. To your knowledge, are you aware of any events in which the special police of Mr. Ecim were involved in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember any specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see him at the police station after the 11th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see Ecim there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you able to observe his behaviour?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a bit arrogant. It was not a man that you could just come up to and talk to him. He was acting in a military fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what was his relationship with Mr. Tepic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of their relations because I cannot remember that I ever saw Mr. Tepic and Mr. Ecim together at a meeting or anything, so I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have one last question, Mr. Raljic. In relation to an answer you gave us yesterday, when we were talking about the communication lines being cut off during the first seven to ten days, do you remember you were asked the same question in your interview?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during our interview three years ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 12399, you answered that after those initial days there were constant shortages of power, almost daily. You repeated it again today. And you told us that in relation to the dispatches the communication lines were unreliable, so you couldn't really be sure that we would be able to send a dispatch at any given moment. You remember you said that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In your interview, you told us that the dispatch communications functioned, although with some difficulty, but under the circumstances, it functioned. Now, could you clarify to the Trial Chamber what was the situation. There was some power outages during the day; but, generally speaking, did the dispatch communication function?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication mostly did not function. So most of the time throughout this period the communication was not functional. I think I said here yesterday that there was a series of circumstances under which we could not send a dispatch. It did not just depend on whether we, at the police station, had power. We depended on the post office and on whether there was power in Banja Luka at any given moment, and, therefore, there were various causes, because of which we could not establish communication. It was just when we had power outages. When I said that we had difficulties, that was precisely what I implied, that sometimes we could not send a dispatch because of all these reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So let me just understand this. You have power outages during the day, and you answered to a question of Judge Harhoff about that. But did we understand you correctly? In the interview you said that generally and understand the circumstances it functioned. So can we understand that even though you had periods during the day when there was no power, after trying or -- during the course of the day you were able to send dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In this period, the communication line mostly did not function. Most of the time it was not functional. If there were power cuts during the day, for example, it depended on the contents of dispatches. There were some dispatches with which we could not wait for five or six days to have the lines functional because it was urgent to do something in connection so then we would send dispatches by other means. Mostly, during this period, the communication lines that we used for sending dispatches did not function properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to wrap it up on this, when you say you would send by other means, what was the other means you would send a dispatch through?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would tell the chief that we could not send a dispatch, and then it was probably sent as part of the courier mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Raljic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we agreed with Mr. Zupljanin Defence that they would go first for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Raljic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. On behalf of the Defence of Stojan Zupljanin, I will ask you some questions today and they are connected to your testimony. As the two of us speak the same language and in order to facilitate other participants to follow the trial and because of the needs for interpretation, please, when you hear my question, take a short break of a few seconds and only then answer the question so that both the question and the answer would be adequately interpreted. You can also follow the transcript in front of you on the screens, so when you see that the line stops, take that into account. I will also try to do that because I speak very quickly and I see that you do so as well. We have to enable the interpreters to do their work properly. Mr. Raljic, when answering to the Prosecutor's questions a while ago, you talked about the relations between Mr. Tepic and the police and the Crisis Staff. You never attended any of the Crisis Staff meetings, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Whether Mr. Tepic submitted any reports or received any orders or any other of the superior members of the police is something that you don't know; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I already answered this question to the Prosecutor. I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you never saw any minutes from the Crisis Staff meetings? That was never submitted to you? When I say this, I imply the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you answered the Prosecutor's questions yesterday, you mentioned a meeting held at the old pensioners' home, when there was talk about signing a loyalty oath which the policemen were supposed to do. You said that the meeting was short and that it was interrupted. The Prosecutor didn't ask you anything further about that specific moment, but I wish to ask you that now. Was it an incident when a group of armed Muslims and Croats came to the meeting and interrupted it? It was a group headed by a Croat called Sprzo. This is the incident that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the reason why that meeting didn't come to its logical end. That group of people led by Stipo Maric called Sprzo forcibly entered the room where the meeting was held at the senior citizens' home they were armed with long-barrelled weapons, and no police officers at the time had such weapons. They had all come to the meeting unarmed. It was a very unpleasant situation. Everybody was afraid for their lives. And everybody ran from that meeting. Everybody ran away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was basically the exerting of pressure of police officers who were Muslims or Croats so as not to join the MUP of the RS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty that it was indeed their motive, but I can assume as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The result was that a number of Muslims and Croats did not sign the solemn declaration and did not join the Serbian MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, at the meeting itself, there was no signing of declarations because the meeting was interrupted by this display of force. It was interrupted violently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor asked you about Muslims and Croats who continued working at the SJB of Kotor Varos, do you know that a number of Muslim -- of Muslims and Croats joined the armed units headed by Mr. Sadikovic and that they established their own unit outside of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there were such members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: While you were speaking about the situation yesterday, answering the Prosecutor's question about the situation in Kotor Varos prior to the 11th of June, 1992, you mentioned that the situation in Kotor Varos was tense. Isn't it true that in that period before the 11th of June, 1992, there were some incidents in Kotor Varos and the surrounding area where the victims were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know -- remember precisely the particular incident. Maybe you can remind me. But I cannot remember that any Serbs were killed before the 11th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some members of the army were disarmed by Muslims and Croats at check-points set up around Muslim and Croat -- Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such cases. One of them on Mount Rujka [phoen] when some guys came from the theatre of war in Croatia, I believe. They were attacked verbally and physically, and the group of armed persons from that village up there, Kotoriste and those villages, came and assembled in front of the police station. They had long-barrelled weapons and protesting why the people had come there. These people had come back from the front line in Croatia. Why they were bothered by that, I don't know. I also remember another incident from May 1992 when, following an agreement with the commander, the deputy, and the chief of the SJB, which was about patrolling the town to provide for security of the citizens because all three ethnic groups wanted that, and we had a van to patrol the suburban settlements in the evening hours. And I remember us going to the village of Vecici which was around 11 p.m. It was dark already. And at a point in time there were some branches, some logs on the road, and the van had to stop. I was present. It was a very unpleasant and tense situation. It was night-time. We were all sitting inside. And I know that in front of the van on the left and on the right there were two armed persons. I remember how one of them looked. He had a beard and long hair. And they pointed their weapons to our van. The driver was a Muslim, a reserve police officer of ours, and they were saying that we had no business entering their village, that they were guarding it, and that we shouldn't come back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also know that immediately before the 11th, in the territory of Kotor Varos municipality, there was a unit, a joint Croatian/Muslim unit which was armed and had radios?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that, before the 11th of June, there was such an organised unit. But people were armed, and they were constantly arming themselves. Because the police, at the time, organised raids at pubs in the villages, and we would often seize weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these Muslims and Croats, apart from the weapons, also had radios to be able to communicate with each other?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I do. At the beginning, I didn't know that they had such equipment. But while I was a civilian, I was a ham radio enthusiast, and I scanned VHF frequencies. And I came across such a radio communication. I intercepted it. As far as I remember, the code-names for the two parties were Skija [phoen] and Zmajl [phoen], and they were exchanging information. Later, I found out that this call-sign of Skija was on Mount Skaljine [phoen], whereas Zmajl was the call-sign of a guy whose name was Mario from Gradiska, which I learned only later. I mean Stara Gradiska in Croatia. There were other radio stations too. It was a developed radio network with call-signs. Their call-signs Vezir, Bedem, Jabuka, Kula, and so on. They had a good network, and I can also add another detail: After Maric, Stipo Maric called Sprzo, was killed in combat, one of the guys brought a piece of paper and gave it to me at the police station. It was their -- it was a table showing the frequencies they used and the hours when they would communicate. And this made my work much easier. Later I was able to track them. But, at any rate, they were well-equipped with radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just another question before the break. You mentioned this man Sprzo. He was killed in the summer of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe in the second half of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether this may be a convenient moment for the pause because I'm about to pass on to another topic, or perhaps we should use another few minutes available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We could as easily take the break at this point. The break this morning is going to be 30 minutes, not 20 minutes, because there may be a technical problem dealing with LiveNote which has to be fixed during the break. So just in case it takes a little longer than 20 minutes, we'll break for 30 minutes, which break we can take now, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to state, for the record, that Mr. Cvijetic joined the Stanisic Defence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, let us continue. The break was a bit longer, due to the problems with the transcript. Yesterday and today, answering the Prosecutor's questions about the number of dispatches received at the centre and about the problems with sending them via the teletype machine, you provided answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to show 65 ter 393. I believe it's an exhibit already, but I don't have the number handy. It's at tab 11. So it's 65 ter 3193. 3193. It's the Prosecution's tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at it, sir. Yesterday, answering the Prosecutor's question, you commented on the last paragraph and said that concerning the communication with Kotor Varos, your -- you were referring to the day of the sending of this report. And that was the 16th of January, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 16th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to page 3 of this document in both the English and the Serbian version -- versions. Can we see the bottom of the page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is stated here that in 1992, as we can read in the last-but-one paragraph, the number of telegrams received and sent is stated, that is, from the 1st of January through 31st of January, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this includes the five months of peacetime; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire year 1992 is taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And there is your comment at the end. It can be observed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: -- the number of dispatches has significantly dropped in relation to the previous year, which, in turn, has been caused by wartime operations in the former BiH, that is, SFRY. That's what the report says; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the period until the 11th of June, 1992, what was the average daily number of incoming and outgoing telegrams, let's say, until the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give precise numbers for that period, but I can give you an example from which we may draw a conclusion. On average, and now I'm referring to the period before the 11th of June to -- 1991 [as interpreted], we had a daily average of about 30 dispatches, which, monthly, would amount to 800 to 1.000 dispatches. So from that we may draw a conclusion as to the time-period you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We can see from this report that there are about 3500 dispatches for the entire year. If we subtract the four or five months of peacetime, this certainly reflects a significantly reduced number of dispatches from the 11th of June on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The language used here is significantly reduced. So it isn't a slight drop but a sharp drop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about individual events today; more specifically, the murder of Ilija Dragulic, then the killings in front of the health centre, medical centre. The information about these events was not sent out through your communications centre; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't send out such information from our communications centre at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the events in the Kotor Varos municipality, such as the burning of the Catholic church and the destruction of some mosques, to the best of your recollection, reports about that were not sent to the CSB through your communications centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you today about the conduct of Chief Tepic when he would receive an order or some sort of letter through the communications centre, whether he acted upon it or not. Let me ask you, as far as you know, did you send detailed reports to multiple recipients? I'm referring to the period after the 11th of June in which you would describe events such as the ones you have just mentioned such as murders, arsons, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such information about such matters was not sent out through our communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit P734.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Defence tab 3; I mean the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this isn't the document. 65 ter 430; and, according to my notes, it's 374.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The police station in Kotor Varos was faced with a loss of personnel so that after the 11th of June they didn't have many professionals; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a loss of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which was reflected in the functioning of the SJB; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And talking about communications, our centre didn't have as many staff as there should have been according to the then-job classification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the -- this letter from the centre in Banja Luka which was sent to all chiefs. And please take a look at page 2 of this document, and will you see Stojan Zupljanin's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here, we see a letter that deals the problem of failures or mistakes made by the SJB: "There are considerable omissions and shortcomings in the daily reports by SJB to the Banja Luka CSB operative duty section on major incidents, which consist of the following ..." And if goes on to say that not all significant event are included, that some information about some events is often incomplete. Then events that -- about which information is received subsequently are not being registered; the offices in charge are practically not even checking the reports. So these are problems that were present not only in Kotor Varos, in their territory, but in the entire territory of the CSB. And then it is stated which elements such reports should include. A template is given. And regard -- with regard to the conditions in Kotor Varos and the combat operations, you didn't apply this template?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the templates. In that period, after the 11th of June, 1992, we never sent anything that was composed in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a look, it says here what a public security station should send in its reports. And if you have a look at items 18 and 19, which are at the bottom, explosions in various facilities, what damage was caused. And then the last line where it says: "Attacks of people of one ethnicity against people of other ethnicity, provide a short description."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then, please, if we could move on to the next page where Mr. Zupljanin requests information under item 24. The number of cases of desecration of monuments, cemeteries and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So such reports were not sent from the Kotor Varos SJB; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that I sent any reports that were made in accordance with this form and with so many items. And the date given at the beginning, as far as I could see, is from the month of May. But I could not see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's the 26th of May. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 26th of May. So this is just ten or 15 days before the beginning of the conflict. And during the summer, as we already mentioned here, we were not able to send, in the morning, the daily reports as I would note, because I think this refers to daily reports. This has to do with daily reporting. And it would be logical for us to send daily reports only 10 or 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you specifically have a look at the last page in item 30(e), Mr. Zupljanin requests that there should be specific reports about war crimes. And through the communications system, in this period, such reports did not pass through your hands, did they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Today, when answering the Prosecutor's questions, you talked about the behaviour of certain groups in Kotor Varos. And when you talked about the reputation which they had, which the specials had, you also had in mind the way they behaved to Chief Tepic. The specials whom you mentioned and who were not behaving properly were the group headed by Slobodan Dubocanin; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had them in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So they are different from the members of the special police who were also present there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Members of the special police unit, as far as I know, wore blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Raljic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Raljic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I only have a few brief questions for you. I wish to clarify one thing with you and to use your professional knowledge to clarify one thing that we need for the transcript and in order to assist the interpreters in future in this case when it comes to interpreting expert matters. My question is the following: Short waves, which is "KT" in B/C/S, are the waves that have frequencies between 3 and 30 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In our language, the abbreviation used for them is "KT."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, KT.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With the help of interpreters, and primarily at their initiative, I managed to find out that the English abbreviation for KT is "HF," which stands for "high frequency." Now, the ultra short waves are those whose frequencies are between 30 and 300 megahertz; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the UKT.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For this abbreviation that we use in our language, namely, "UKT," the abbreviation which is used in English is "VHF," which stands for "very high frequency."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. VHF stands for very high frequency. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I think that we have clarified that now. Let me ask you this: I think that during your interview with the Prosecution you discussed this. Do you know what was the ethnic composition of the Dabovci village which is situated in the vicinity of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it a Muslim or a Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very centre of Dabovci is a Serbian village. It's located along the main road. Dabovci, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in mid-August 1992 the Serbian army attacked the Dabovci village razed it to the ground?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. My grandfather used to live in Dabovci. My uncle is living in Dabovci today, together with his family. It's along the main road. And all these houses in Dabovci are in tact. Now whether this is just a hamlet which is in the outlining areas of Dabovci, I wouldn't know. But as for the Dabovci village themselves, it's a place populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, this is a Adjudicated Fact 943.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, do you know someone called Predrag Markovic from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How about Marinko Djukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know one Marinko Djuric but not Marinko Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Markovic and Mr. Djukic were members of the police, you should know them or at least be familiar with their names; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we can say with a high degree of certainty that neither Mr. Markovic nor Mr. Marinko Djukic were members of the police or that they had any command positions or authority within the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the information of -- to the Trial Chamber, this is Adjudicated Fact 515.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I think that it was yesterday during the examination-in-chief when you talked about the 11th of June, 1992, in Kotor Varos. If I understood your testimony correctly, you said that on the 11th of June the situation was as it was but that there were no conflicts which took place on that date.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 11th of June, or in the month of June in general, did the Bosnian Serb army mount any attacks on the town of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the entire town of Kotor Varos at the very beginning. So counting from the 11th of June and on the following few days there was no armed conflict at all. As far as I know, people were handing over their weapons, especially in the village Zabrdje, Podbrdje, and Slatina, because all the houses located there remained intact and no one harassed these people at all. In the first few days, there was no conflict. I think that the main conflict began after the incident that I mentioned after a hand grenade was thrown at the young men in the Kotor settlement. I think that the conflict escalated somewhat after that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the conflicts had to do, as you said, with the Kotor settlement, so it is a place that is, in fact, outside Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in Kotor Varos, but it is located across the Vrbanja river.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that if there were any attacks against the Vetici [phoen], Hrvacani, Ravne, and Hanicici [phoen] villages in the month of June 1992 and that these attacks were carried out by the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain if there were any during the month of June. Later on during the summer there were such conflicts, but I think that there were no situations like that during the month of June. I know that some men were sent to these villages during June in order to talk to these people because the villagers were armed. So some people were sent over there to suggest to these people that they should hand over their weapons and so that the situation would be resolved in a peaceful manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To inform the Trial Chamber that this is the Adjudicated Fact 519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In line 38 [sic] 5, the name of the village is not on the record. People were handing over their weapons especially in the village ... and Slatina. Could we clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please be so kind to repeat your answer, which has not been recorded. I asked you if on 11th of June or during the month of June, in general, the members of the Bosnian Serb army mounted any attacks against Kotor Varos, the town itself. You said: Not against the whole town in the beginning. And if we count from the 11th of June and on the following several days, there were no conflicts at all. As far as I know, people were handing over their weapons, especially in the villages - and the villages have not been recorded - the names of the villages and Slatina village, because all the houses there remained intact and no one harassed these people at all. Can you please just repeat the name of this village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are villages Podbrdje, Zabrdje, and Slatina. These are villages located along the main road leading from Kotor Varos to Banja Luka. There may have been isolated incidents in which some house or other was torched, but there were no conflicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. Just for the record, Mr. Zecevic was referred to Adjudicated Fact 515. That one refers to another municipality, not to Kotor Varos. I believe it's Teslic, just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell us if you're familiar with a certain Goran Zaric from Kotor Varos, if you know that name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any Goran Zaric, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He has a nickname: Dziba or Djiba.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djiba. That can be Goran Zaric, not Goran Zharic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So are you familiar with the name of Goran Zaric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that he was in the police reserves, as far as I can remember. Or he could have been in active service, an active policeman; I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about Zdravko Zutic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Zutic, I am familiar with that name, but he wasn't an active-duty policeman. I think he was in the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And do you know a certain Dusko Vujicic from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he's actually from Banja Luka. He worked in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what did he do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- actually, I already asked about the village of Dabovci and you explained that this was a mostly Serb-inhabited village and some members of your family also live in that village. Do you know that Bosnian Serb forces frequently robbed Bosnian Muslims' homes in the village of Dabovci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the village of Dabovci, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you probably went to visit your family and you stayed in touch with them during 1992. Did they tell you that Muslim homes in the village of Dabovci would be frequently robbed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never talked about that. Nobody ever said anything about that. None of my relatives ever did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber, this is Adjudicated Fact 542. Mr. Raljic, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just a few questions for re-examination, Your Honours. I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, you were asked at the beginning of the cross-examination by Mr. Krgovic about a man nicknamed Sprzo. Can I ask you, first of all, was he a local from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us - I don't know if the transcript is correct - that he was killed in combat. Do you know the exact circumstances of his death?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What were those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stipo Maric, Sprzo, was killed in armed conflict at Stara Kula, the old tower in Kotor Varos, where the army and the specials had a conflict with the Muslim/Croat forces. I know that on this occasion Serbs who fought there got killed, and as far as I know, 10 or 12 members of the Muslim/Croatian forces were also killed. So it was armed conflict and as far as I know, they were all killed in conflict. Stipo Maric, Sprzo, was a member of some Croatian units. I once intercepted a conversation in which he requested from the person he was talking to in Gradiska that he should get in touch with some different brigade of theirs that he was a member of, which was located in Dugo Selo in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You didn't take part in that armed conflict, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You didn't see whether Mr. Maric was killed right there, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I can explain, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What I'm interested in finding out is: You were not present when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically I was not present. It wouldn't have been logical either because he was on the other side. But on the next day I saw him dead, after that clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Where did you see him dead?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the army took control over that part of town, they brought in the people they found there and among them there was a Maric, also known as Sprzo. I saw him lying on the road on a ground-sheet. And among the people who were killed -- who were killed, there was a Marko Jelasic, also known as Bato, who went to school with me. He got killed on that day. And a man by the name of Jadranko. There was a list of ten or 12 people, and, among them, they mentioned also the name of Stipo Maric, also known Sprzo, as having been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't think witness's answer was recorded properly because I believe he mentioned that some of the information he got, he got from the intercept. So maybe you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Also on clarification, the status of this guy, his fellow, friend from school, because he mentioned he was member of some unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In relation to the first intervention, not quite sure the issue about the intercept. You received some information about this Maric through an intercept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it's about, and that was the information I learned in the evening hours of the same day. I believe it was late July. A short while ago, we discussed this topic, and I also engaged in electronic surveillance or reconnaissance, and that's how I found out, when they mentioned the list of all people who got killed there. Among them there was there person called Marko Jelasic, nicknamed Bato, which Mr. Krgovic wanted me to explain. He was a member of the reserve police force. But there was also Nedim Zehir, nicknamed Bajs; he also attended primary school with me, and I believe he was also a reserve police officer.
