utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when the name of Sprzo was mentioned, it was in relation to the signing of the loyalty oath which you said was, at that point, interrupted. Did there come a time when eventually the loyalty oaths were signed by the members of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. This all happened in a very short period of time. That incident took place maybe in mid-May, and I -- in the following days, the situation was very tense. So I don't know whether or not the loyalty oath was signed at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. And just to be clear, did you yourself ever sign that loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I may have. But it was a formality, something that I simply don't remember. I may have. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Krgovic about the individual events that we spoke about this morning, the killing of Mr. Dragulic and the killings in front of the hospital, and he asked you whether you sent any dispatches about those events and your answer was that you couldn't remember sending any dispatches for those events. The chief of the police station, was he duty-bound to report killings to the superiors?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, in such a situation, I don't know; it's difficult to say whether he was duty-bound, from today's vantage point. It was -- there was a war on. People were getting killed. So it was -- it would have been naive to expect for the police to go out in the field and conduct on-site investigations with bullets flying around. And so I don't know whether he was duty-bound to report such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Maybe if I question it this way: In relation to the rules within the police, is the police chief to report any important events, such as a murder, in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you said that you didn't send -- you don't remember sending a dispatch. Do you rule out the possibility that a report may have been sent by courier?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he's calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The issue is whether a dispatch was sent or not. I'm just asking the witness to see if he rules out the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Ask him directly: Did he have any knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Demirdjian, anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Right. That's all the questions I have, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you mentioned fact -- Adjudicated Fact 943 in regard to Dabovci village. You were asking the witness whether he knew about destruction of that village, but adjudicated fact -- I suppose, you mentioned it because you're challenging it? 943.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- but I don't think I mentioned number 943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, then it's -- then it's not good in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- that's correct. Yes, 943. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the first adjudicated fact that I was challenging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- so you asked the witness about the destruction of that village --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- but adjudicated facts -- the adjudicated fact is about a killing; when people were taken to a nearby place and where somebody executed, by the soldiers. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But obviously the witness was not aware, so I didn't push it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it's only --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't went that far. But, Your Honours, with all due respect, it says: "At least three Bosnian Muslim men from Dabovci were killed after Bosnian Serb soldiers had destroyed their village in mid-August 1992." So that is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So your challenge is about the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, something was recorded in the transcript when I requested an explanation. This witness spoke about people being killed as members of the reserve police force. Perhaps it would be good to ask the witness on which side these people, his school-time friends were killed, were -- on which side they were at the moment they got killed. That wasn't reflected in the transcript. So maybe that could be elicited from the witness. Because he merely needs to finish his answer, because he was cut off by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... well, you -- you could put the question, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, when you were speaking about those school-time friends of yours who were members of the reserve police force and got killed, they were members of the reserve police force before 11th, the reserve police force of the SJB of Kotor Varos, and then later on they joined the Muslim Croat armed units and they were killed as members of the Muslim Croat armed units; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RALJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Raljic, we thank you for your testimony before the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I thank you. And if I may say that I cooperated well, both with the Prosecution and with the two Defence teams, and I hope that my testimony here will contribute to finding the truth and passing a fair judgement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had asked to have five minutes at the end of day to raise a couple of matters, and one of those matters relates to the scheduling. The next witness is being proofed and I understand is not ready to begin testifying until tomorrow morning at 9.00. We had a Defence estimate, I think, of a total of five hours for cross-examination. And as you've seen, it was much reduced. Ms. Pidwell tells me by e-mail she had asked the Defence to review their estimates just to help us with scheduling, but that's the situation we're in. So my first request is that we adjourn for the day and resume with the next witness tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You said that's your first request. You have another request?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. The other matter, Your Honour, I wanted to raise something in conjunction with the order issued by the Trial Chamber yesterday in relation to the Mladic notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat what you just said, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to raise something in conjunction with your order issued yesterday in relation to the Mladic notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, you've given the Prosecution an order to provide certain materials by the 12th of July, or, if we're unable to do so, to provide you a report. The first matter is to provide English translations of the portions of the notebooks that we submit are prima facie relevant and that we seek to add to our exhibit list, and the second is to provide information and material supporting that prima facie authenticity. Well, certainly, number two we will certainly do. We have some additional materials we can provide to you immediately. And I'll check and see if we have even more beyond that. That's not a problem. The first part, relating to identifying -- relates to the part of the order asking us to identify with specificity the portions of the notebooks we seek to add. And in your order at page 4, the paragraph says: "Considering also that the Prosecution has not identified with the required specificity the portions of the notebooks that it seeks to add to the exhibit list." And then the footnote is footnote 18; it makes reference to the Prlic case. We do note there's a difference in the status of this case from Prlic. Prlic is in the status where the Prosecution has rested its case long ago and is now seeking to reopen its case and introduce this evidence. We say that's a distinction that should make a difference. Here, the Prosecution case is ongoing. We haven't completed our case yet. And we think, as evidence develops, it may change our views about which portions of the notebooks we need to use. You've seen from the submission the notebooks covered, I think, the period from 1991 to 1996. It's my understanding I think we now have complete English translations for 1992. And, in our view, the entire set of notebooks for 1992 is something that we would seek to add to our list. Perhaps portions of 1991 and 1993. But we haven't been able to fully review the translations that are available up to date to give you that entire breakdown. I understand the Trial Chamber's reluctance to have thousands of pages that may not be necessary or pertinent. But the nature of these documents, contemporaneous accounts kept by one of the members of the JCE, a high-ranking member of the JCE, we think, for example, the 1992 notebooks should come in, in their entirety. Because it's likely that in the course of trial - bear with me - it's likely that in the course of trial matters -- if we only select excerpts, I can tell you, Your Honours, from my experience with other similar kinds of things like meeting notes of the army that I had in another case with Mr. Zecevic and Mr. O'Sullivan, that if we only have excerpts it will become apparent during the trial that additional excerpts now need to be added because something of a witness said or another new document that came in. We would be having repeated requests probably by both parties to add additional portions. I would suggest the better course is to have the entire document in. The parties will make their submissions at the end of the case about which portions are relevant, pertinent, and should be relied upon by you, but you can ignore the rest or give it no weight. But it's -- it puts it in context and it relates to the matters that were going on at the time. Be that as it may, Your Honour, however, at this point what we're asking is simply to add these to our exhibit list. We're not seeking to introduce them into evidence yet. I think that time will come for certainly some portions of the diary, probably not all. But, at this stage, we think all you need to decide is whether or not we can add them to our list. And in your order I think you have found that we've shown good cause for the late discovery and presentation of this evidence, something clearly outside our control; they were only found earlier this year, and we've tried to move expeditiously to bring them to your attention and to the Defence. I see Judge Harhoff has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well -- thank you, Mr. Hannis. My comment was that in your motion you had requested admission to the 65 ter list of all the notebooks covering the entire period from 1991 to 1996. And the Chamber ruled that that is simply too much; you have to select. If you are seeking now to select the portions from 1992, I think that would be well within the limits of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, I would say that 1992 is -- is a portion of the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That could be a portion of the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's helpful. I think one reading that we took was that it was to go through 1992, it's 383 pages, find me two pages and two lines, et cetera. Thank you, that's helpful. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if I may add, Mr. Hannis, the other thing that we sought to convey in the ruling in the language we chose was to point out the obvious, that the -- after you would have overcome the handicap of having to have the material translated, you would then be in a position to know, even within, say, 1992, that time-frame, what is helpful. So the language, we thought, was sufficiently liberal to erase any apprehensions that you have now expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all very helpful, Your Honour. And I think one of our concerns was not being able yet to have English translations of the entire collection. And perhaps there's a possibility there might be something in 1994, 1995, or 1996 that were retrospective. But we were concerned that if it's not on our list and by the time we get it translated and analysed and we have something, then we'll be up against a tougher argument to say, Oh, now we want to add something from 1995. But I think we've aired the matter. I have -- I certainly, personally, have a better understanding of what you intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, even if that would happen, wouldn't that eventually not be a good cause to ask an additional [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I would certainly argue that, and I hope so, and I'm happy to hear that. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours. We cited our concerns already in our submissions on the subject. However, there is one thing that -- that I'm aware of and I know my friends from the Office of the Prosecutor are aware of, but -- but it is -- it is causing some additional concern for the Defence. Namely, we are informed that the -- that from the same source we are to expect a number of video and audio material, and it has been disclosed to some other Defences in this Tribunal. Now, I am -- I'm really concerned about the amount of that material. And I mentioned that with my talks with Ms. Korner on a number of occasions, and she informed me that -- that the material has been received in the -- in the Office of the Prosecutor, but -- but at that -- at that point - I think it was almost a month ago - the Office of the Prosecutor was asking a Dutch forensic lab to help them -- I don't know, something technologically -- help to copy that material or something along those lines. I'm not really sure. And I ask for your pardon for that because I'm not -- I wasn't really prepared for this. But I'm just -- I'm just making this observation. And maybe we can hear if my learned friend Mr. Hannis can give us an update on this -- on the status of this material. If -- if not today, maybe in the -- in the course of next few days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the Chamber is only aware of an application for introduction of the notebooks. And now Mr. Zecevic informs us that, apparently, in the process of seizing those notebooks, some other material also came to light and that this other material is also in the picture. This is news to us. Can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have to proceed with the caveat that I'm not fully informed about the full extent of this. But it's my understanding that at the time the notebooks were found there were additional materials found including some audio tapes like some of the, sort of, mini-cassettes that were used in little Dictaphone recorders that were popular many years ago. And I believe there was some video as well. They appear to be related -- at least some of that material appears to be related to the notebooks. It's my understanding that some of the notebooks, where there's a meeting recorded, on occasion there is a reference, handwritten, that makes reference to "tape-recorded." So -- and some of the tame recordings have a label on them that suggest they may be related to some entry in the written notebook. As Mr. Zecevic indicated, that material, because it's old and there's a concern about the integrity of the actual tapes themselves, that's why the OTP has consulted with the Dutch forensic institute to help analyse that material, see if it can be copied without destroying it, et cetera. And that's what's in process. It's my understanding that some of the that material, perhaps a copy of it, I'm not even sure, was disclosed in Prlic because of the urgent nature of the status of that case and the Prosecution's request to open the case. I -- I certainly will try and investigate what the status of that is and inform the Defence and -- as well as the Chamber. At this point in time, we didn't know enough about that material to include it our application. Although, on the face, it seems it may be related, and we may want to make that application. But, frankly, I just don't know yet. I hope that answers your question, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- sorry. I was going to say, the last observation that you made, Mr. Hannis, about communicating with the Defence is exactly what I was going to suggest, in terms of Mr. Zecevic's request, that one would think that, as with everything else, that counsel on both sides continue their working relationship outside of court. And the Chamber need only be involved when it has to make a formal pronouncement on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I should indicate, with reference to my remarks about what was disclosed in Prlic, in relation to the audio and video materials, was a list of those materials, not any actual recordings. I think it was just an indication of what they appeared to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So if there's nothing else, we'll take the adjournment to -- I think we're still in this courtroom tomorrow. Yes, 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day Of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.05 p.m.,
